chunks: From him, from a man who said:

I wrote to the Jurist (peace be upon him) regarding a man who bought half of a house, undivided, from another man, and his partner, who owned the other half, was absent. When he took possession and moved out, the house collapsed, and a torrential flood came and destroyed it and carried it away. Then his absent partner came and claimed the right of pre-emption (shuf'ah) from this man. He gave him the pre-emption, on the condition that he return his money in full, which he had paid for its price. He said to him: 'Reduce from me the value of the construction, for the construction has collapsed and the flood has taken it away.' What is obligatory in that matter? So he (peace be upon him) issued a ruling: 'He has nothing but the first sale and purchase, if God wills.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on pre-emption when the co-owned property is destroyed by natural disaster?
ai.summary: In this ruling from the *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that in cases of *shuf'ah* (pre-emption) for undivided property, the pre-emptor steps into the shoes of the original buyer, bearing the risk of loss (*ghurm*) alongside the gain (*ghunm*). This establishes that the pre-emptor must pay the full original price without deducting for the destroyed structure, reflecting the principle that the pre-emption effectively reverts the transaction to its initial state. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential view that pre-emption is not a new purchase but a substitution in the existing contract.
